title: This Low-ABV Breakfast Spritz Tastes Like the Amalfi Coast
summary:
The refreshing low-proof Breakfast Spritz served at Casa Angelina in Praiano, Italy, is made with tea, Sherry, lemon, and honey.

The post This Low-ABV Breakfast Spritz Tastes Like the Amalfi Coast appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Perhaps it was only a matter of time before spritzes conquered breakfast. 

The Breakfast Spritz, an herbal, slightly sweet cocktail garnished with local honeycomb, is one of the most popular cocktails served at Casa Angelina, a luxe hotel located in the cliffs of Praiano on the Amalfi Coast. Made with English breakfast tea, Sherry, honey, and fresh lemon, the spritz is refreshing, earthy, and invigorating all at once, with an even lower abv than your standard spritz.

“Our classic cocktails are still very popular, but we’ve seen more and more guests showing interest in lower-alcohol drinks,” says bartender Marco Giordano, who developed the recipe for the hotel’s Seascape Bar. Overlooking the Tyrrhenian Sea, with views of Positano and Capri framed by oversized windows, the elegant all-white bar offers guests a dedicated spritz menu, which includes a section for lower-alcohol options, as well as Champagne spritzes and an array of Italian riffs. 

“Tea, honey, and lemon are all typical breakfast flavors, and we wanted to reinterpret them in a light, refreshing cocktail,” says Giordano. This year, the property introduced beehives into its cliffside garden, which supplies the honey for the drink. In fact, most of the ingredients for the cocktails at Seascape Bar are sourced from its steep garden, which climbs almost vertically to the sky and also provides the hotel with tomatoes, herbs, eggs, and seasonal produce. 

Despite its name, guests mostly order the cocktail in the afternoon. “It’s actually most popular by the pool,” says Giordano. “Guests usually order it during the afternoon while relaxing in the sun. It’s light, refreshing, and easy to drink, which makes it perfect for the Amalfi Coast climate.”

The Breakfast Spritz

From bartender Marco Giordano

Ingredients

⅓ ounce Sherry
2 ⅓ ounces of English Breakfast tea
⅓ ounce honey
⅓ ounce fresh lemon juice
2 ounces soda water
Optional garnishes: fresh mint, honeycomb, Maraschino cherry

Instructions

  1. Dissolve the honey in the fresh lemon juice. 
  2. Pour into a large wine glass, add the Sherry and chilled English Breakfast tea, then stir gently. 
  3. Fill the glass with ice and top with soda water. Garnish with a small piece of honeycomb, a cherry, and a sprig of fresh mint.

  • Look out Aperol: Sarti Rosa has landed in America.
  • The Honey Deuce has some competition. Enter, the Watermelon Slice.
  • If you’re ready for the fall vibes, the Unknown Vegetable is just right.

title: The Best Wines for Every Zodiac Sign
summary:
Should we be looking to the stars when picking a wine?

The post The Best Wines for Every Zodiac Sign appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Love it or think it’s ridiculous, astrology has increasingly worked its way into popular culture and the general psyche.

Major magazines, from Cosmopolitan and Elle to Vogue and GQ, regularly cover the topic, publishing horoscopes and articles about how the planets are impacting various aspects of life. Social media is full of astrological influencers. Pop artists, like Kacey Musgraves, SZA, and Ariana Grande, have sung about Saturn and its return in their music.

According to a survey of 2,000 young Americans, around 80% of all Gen Z and millennials believe in astrology—a significant portion of whom use the practice to make career and other major life decisions.

This got us wondering: Should we be looking to the stars when picking a wine, too?

Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Tonya Pitts thinks so.

“I am a firm believer that everything is connected and people gravitate to people, places, and things that spark something inside them; it could be joy, passion, intrigue, or memories from the past,” she says. “There are those that say it has nothing to do with anything, but I like to think it’s all in the stars and planetary alignments.”

To help guide the various zodiac signs toward specific wine that may resonate with their various attributes, Pitts took into account the general flavor profiles of grape varietals and along with regional attributes. Then, she sought out bottles that evoke emotion and translate into traits of behaviors of the signs, essentially thinking if a varietal were a person, what would it taste like and what sort of emotions would it produce?

“It’s no simple formula,” she adds. While she did her best to map it all out, Pitts admits, “every prediction or thought doesn’t line up with everyone either.”

So, what, precisely, are her astrological wine picks? Check them out below.

Aries (March 21 – April 19): Syrah

Themes: “Bold and ambitious, Aries dives headfirst into even the most challenging situations—and they’ll make sure they always come out on top,” says Pitts.

Why: “Syrah is bold and ambitious, like an Aries. Often a sleeper hit, it’s a wine that always strives to stand out, much like those born under this sign. Syrah is grown around the globe. It is always fantastic and intriguing, much like the ram.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Pursued by Bear 2022 Baby Bear Syrah (Columbia Valley (WA))

Baby Bear is a perfect name for this Syrah, as I consider it a “Goldilock’s wine” where everything is just right. The first aroma to catch your attention is pure blackberry pie. The fruit is followed by puffs of mint and pork chops roasting over a salty driftwood fire at the beach. Black cherry and espresso flavors are joined by the tiniest bit of anise. This Baby Bear hibernated for 30 months in 17% new and 83% used 600L puncheons. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — Michael Alberty

$58 Wine.com

Château de Nages 2021 JT Syrah (Costières de Nîmes)

Composed of 95% Syrah and 5% Mourvèdre, this wine opens with blackberry and kirsch compote, dried thyme, violets, black peppercorn and earthy depth on the nose. Energetic and juicy, it delivers ample blackberry fruit with an edge of white pepper. Silky yet powerful, it finishes long making it a good companion for layered dishes such as moussaka. 92 Points — Anna-Christina Cabrales

$30 Total Wine & More

Taurus (April 20 – May 20): Mourvèdre

Themes: “Tauruses are oriented around the physical world,” says Pitts. “Bulls tend to be grounded and logical. They love routine and they’re committed to their own comfort.”

Why: “Mourvèdre is a grounded and supple wine, mirroring Taurus’s love for routine and comfort. Known for its floral notes and dark fruit flavors like blackberry and boysenberry, Mourvèdre is both forceful and subtle, making it a perfect match for the grounded nature of a Taurus.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Stiekema 2024 Mourvèdre (Paso Robles)

This blend of Calesta and Kiler Canyon vineyards is a lavish and detailed style of Mourvèdre, starting with dark cherry and woodspice aromas on the nose. The palate is bold and expressive, offering blackberry, dark cherry, nutmeg, and woodspice flavors. 94 Points — Matt Kettmann

$54 Stiekema

Miraflores Winery 2023 Estate Mourvèdre (El Dorado County)

Aromatic with notes of wild black strawberries, raspberries, dried rose petals, coriander, grilled orange zest, and French oak on the nose; the palate is bright mulberries, dark plums, cassis, pink grapefruit, dried chicory and supple tannins to finish. 93 Points — Tonya Pitts

$38 Miraflores Winery

Gemini (May 21 – June 20): Riesling

Themes: “Spontaneous, playful, and adorably erratic, Geminis are driven by their insatiable curiosity,” says Pitts. “Appropriately symbolized by the celestial twins, this air sign is interested in so many pursuits that it had to double itself.”

Why: “Just like Gemini, Riesling has many faces (and no, that’s not a bad thing). Whether it’s dry or rich with residual sugar, Riesling embodies the duality and versatility of a Gemini, making it an exciting and unpredictable choice that can vary widely depending on where it’s grown.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Fess Parker 2024 Rodney’s Vineyard Riesling (Santa Barbara County)

Classic petrol aromas are cut by lemon sorbet and coconut flake on the nose of this bottling. The palate is racy and texture, pairing brisk Meyer lemon peel flavors with tangerine sorbet and more petrol touches. This should last long. Drink now-2044. Cellar Selection. 94 Points — M.K.

$25 Solano Cellars

Weingut Karl Erbes 2023 Üziger Würzgarten Auslese Riesling (Mosel)

Layered and expressive, with orange blossom, ripe peach, quince, and a hint of tropical fruit forming a generous core. Floral notes and gentle spice add nuance throughout. The sweetness is well-balanced by lively acidity, giving the wine lift and precision. Slightly more restrained in intensity, it still delivers a long, complex finish with elegant persistence. 92 Points — Aleks Zecevic

$35 Plum Market

Cancer (June 21 – July 22): Cabernet Franc

Themes: “Nurturing and loyal, Cancers are also protective of their loved ones,” says Pitts. “They are highly sensitive, deeply caring, and feel everything deeply.”

Why: “Cabernet Franc is nurturing and needs careful attention, just like a Cancer. Depending on how it’s grown, it can range from herbaceous and red-fruited to deep, dark and brooding, reflecting the crab’s depth of emotion and sensitivity.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Domaine de la Petite Roche 2022 Cabernet Franc (Anjou)

This is a gorgeous wine. Perfumed aromas of raspberry-blossom, rosehip, dried-cherry flakes and violet open on the nose followed by black olive and boysenberry. Supple tannins guide a well-integrated mix of red-and-black fruit along a roller-coaster ride of flavors that are showered in pencil shavings, forest floor and dried hay. Best Buy. 92 Points — Reggie Solomon

$19 Union Square Wines & Spirits

Darcie Kent Vineyards 2023 Lemmons Vineyard Cabernet Franc (San Francisco Bay-Livermore Valley)

Livermore Valley has a treasure trove of Cabernet Franc offerings. stylistically, there is an expression that pleases everyone’s palate; this one is concentrated on the nose, with aromas of bramble black currant, black plum, coriander, cedar, and sagebrush. The flavors on the palate are ripe, red plum, cassis, dark cherry, bittersweet chocolate, star anise, and supple tannins on the finish. 92 Points — T.P.

$55 Darcie Kent Vineyards

Leo (July 23 – August 22): Cabernet Sauvignon

Themes: “Passionate, loyal, and infamously dramatic, Leo is represented by the lion and these spirited fire signs are the kings and queens of the celestial jungle,” says Pitts.

Why: “Cabernet Sauvignon is often seen as the king of wines, much like Leo’s place in the zodiac. Known for its boldness and stature in the wine world, the varietal commands attention and is a top choice for a sign that loves to be in the spotlight.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Le Roi 2024 Le Roi Rouge Cabernet Sauvignon Cabernet Sauvignon (Pays d’Oc)

This would be a superb wine at three times the price, offering far more in flavor, texture and stability than most anything in its price class. Deep aromas of blackberry, peppercorn, woodspice and oregano lead from the nose into a rich palate that’s lush but bone dry. Flavors of blue and red fruit are dusted in espresso and baking spice, finishing on a chocolate note. Best Buy. 94 Points — M.K.

$17 Taylor’s Wine Shop

Merriam Vineyards 2021 Gloeckner-Turner Ranch Cabernet Sauvignon (Rockpile)

This dark and rich Cabernet displays intense aromas of reduced berries, plum compote, violets and ginger on the nose. The palate is plush and velvety, with long, smooth tannin, juicy acidity and flavors of raspberry gastrique, blueberry jam, black pepper and herbal potpourri that dances along the finish. Gorgeous now, this will benefit from some time in the cellar. Best 2030-2050. Cellar Selection. 95 Points — Tom R. Capo

$88 Merriam Vineyards

Virgo (August 23 – September 22): Grüner Veltliner

Themes: “Virgos are said to be the most analytical and organized members of the zodiac, as foxes are logical, practical, and systematic in their approach to life,” says Pitts.

Why: “Grüner Veltliner is complex and layered, much like a Virgo. Its pleasing and intricate flavors require attention to detail, making it the ideal wine for this meticulous and practical sign.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Anarchist Wine Co. 2023 The Anarchist Grüner Veltliner (Mokelumne River)

This expression has tossed out the rule about perception and has embraced a what and where I can fit into your daily routine, whether food-wise or kicking back. We are here for it! The aromatics are bright and rich, with a concentration of White nectarine, peach, baked apples, and honeysuckle. At the same time, the palate gallops into White grapefruit, tangerine, turmeric, lifted acidity, and a mouth-watering finish. 92 Points — T.P.

$26 Anarchist Wine Co.

Nittnaus 2022 Elektra Grüner Veltliner (Weinland Österreich)

Exceptionally complex and layered, this wine unfolds with white raspberry, yellow apple, and delicate quince blossom. Vibrant kumquat-like acidity adds tension, while a subtle bitter-sweet undertone enhances the depth. Silky texture, multilayered flavors, and a persistent, long finish make this a truly captivating expression. 94 Points — A.Z.

$20 Union Square Wines & Spirits

Libra (September 23 – October 22): Sauvignon Blanc

Themes: “Libras are known for the love of being around other people. They are a fun and loving extroverted sign,” says Pitts.

Why: “Sauvignon Blanc is a bright and lively wine that makes you want to bask in the sun, just like these swans love being in the company of others. Its fresh and approachable nature reflects Libras’ love of socializing and fun.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Domaine Roc de l’Abbaye 2024 Sauvignon Blanc (Sancerre)

This wine has a flowery, complex nose that draws you in with muddled green pear and keeps you there with aromas of dried hay and lemon blossom. The stony palate boasts vibrant minerality that is in sync with Gala apple on the lengthy palate. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — R.S.

$39 Wine.com

Jules Taylor 2025 Sauvignon Blanc (Marlborough)

This vintage of veteran winemaker Jules Taylor’s classic SB is singing. Bright and bouncy, with passionfruit, lemon-lime, pink grapefruit, fresh tarragon, and basil aromas. The palate is zippy and fresh, a shooting star of acidity amidst an intriguing creamy-pithy texture combo, with a wild edge to the long herb-flecked citrus finish that makes the mouth water for more. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Christina Pickard

$20 Wine.com

Scorpio (October 23 – November 21): Pinot Noir

Themes: “Elusive and mysterious, Scorpio is one of the most misunderstood signs of the zodiac,” says Pitts. “Scorpions are known for their loyalty and devotion—and also their passion.”

Why: “Pinot Noir is often misunderstood, just like Scorpio. It’s a delicate, thin-skinned grape that requires nurturing, but when treated with care, it can be deeply rewarding. Its reputation for being dark and complex mirrors Scorpio’s passionate and enigmatic nature.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Bob Cabral Wines 2022 Cuvée Electric Hippy Pinot Noir (Sonoma Coast)

Explosive aromas of pomegranate molasses, cranberry compote, Darjeeling, nori and roses burst from the glass on the nose of this enticing Pinot. The palate delivers flavors of concentrated Bing cherry, licorice, cinnamon and orange peel in a framework of powder-fine tannin and voluptuous acidity. Brilliant now, this will benefit from some time in the cellar. Best from 2030-2040. Editors’ Choice. 97 Points — T.R.C.

$125 Bob Cabral Wines

Bader-Mimeur 2022 Château de Chassagne-Montrachet Pinot Noir (Chassagne-Montrachet)

This wine feels like the moment after a lover’s quarrel, powerful, seductive and impossible to ignore. The nose is heady with rose petal, iodine, charred meat, black peppercorn, violet, white pepper and fine herbs. Silky on the palate, it carries floral spice and white tea through a long finish. Delicious now, or cellar through 2035. 93 Points — A.C.C.

$56 Wine.com

Sagittarius (November 22 – December 21): Grenache

Themes: “What makes Sagittarius so unique is its dynamic blend of passion, curiosity, intensity, and adaptability,” says Pitts. “The centaur values independence and the ability to do what they want, when they want, above all else.”

Why: “Grenache is versatile and adaptable, much like a Sagittarius. It can stand on its own but also blends well with others, reflecting Sagittarius’s independent yet social nature. Grenache is a perfect match for this adventurous and passionate sign.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

La Lomita Wines 2023 Islay Hill Vineyard Grenache (Edna Valley)

Lavish aromas of boysenberry, raspberry sorbet and alluring baking spice show on the layered, complex and exciting nose of this bottling from an estate that sits on one of the appellation’s volcanic plugs. That strawberry and cherry core is awash in French toast spices, loving rich and bold yet still fresh. 97 Points — M.K.

$68 La Lomita

Capricorn (December 22 – January 19): Aglianico

Themes: “Capricorns are known to be extremely hardworking visionaries, leaders, and trailblazers,” says Pitts. “Pragmatic and proud, sea goats want to be praised both for the reasonable actions they take and their approach to life.”

Why: “Aglianico is a grape that matures into something truly special. Grown in mountainous regions, it starts off with iron-rich, dry red fruit flavors and develops into a solid, earthy wine that leaves a lasting impression, embodying the determination and visionary spirit of a Capricorn.”

Explore more great wines for Capricorns here.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Fontanavecchia 2019 Vigna Cataratte Riserva Aglianico (Aglianico del Taburno)

The nose opens with the warm spiciness of terracotta, oregano and sun-dried tomato, then sweetens with ripe berries layered with salted dark chocolate. The palate is tangy with pomegranate and black plum, before more herbs and bitter chocolate recall the nose. Tannins are decisive but not aggressive, and allow a cooling, minty salinity to play out on the finish. A flex from Fontanavecchia, as this wine undeniably overdelivers. 94 Points — Danielle Callegari

$44 Wine Watch

Monte Volpe 2020 Aglianico (Mendocino County)

The spectrum of Italian varietals grown in California is astounding and plentiful. This one is showing up more often, and it is Aglianico. Unlike its version grown in Italy, the fruit is rich, vibrant dark berries with a softer tannin structure and much more ready to drink even with fuller tannins. It is an absolute match for hearty meals like grilled and roasted meat dishes. 93 Points — Tonya Pitts

$40 Graziano Family Of Wines

Aquarius (January 20 – February 18): Viognier

Themes: “Aquarians are clever, analytical, technical, truthful, assertive, confident, progressive, and innovative,” says Pitts. “These water bearers like to solve problems, improve what’s already working well and push boundaries.” 

Why: “Viognier is a thoughtful and complex wine that, when done right, can be very thought-provoking, just like an Aquarius. Whether blended with Syrah to add a floral touch or enjoyed on its own, Viognier’s ability to stand out reflects Aquarius’s innovative spirit.”

Explore more wines for Aquarians here.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Yalumba 2023 The Virgilius Viognier (Eden Valley)

An oh-so-Viognier perfume lures the senses with heady notes of honeysuckle, cherry blossom, a white peach, lemon curd and white pepper. One you manage to pry your nostrils from the glass to take a sip, you’re met with a fulsome, mouth-filling palate that’s creamy but never heavy or syrupy, those floral and fruit notes flowing more subtly to the finish. Pair with buttered chicken or a Thai curry. 94 Points — C.P.

$50 Wine.come

Cedarville Vineyard 2023 Estate Viognier (El Dorado)

The aromas are lush, with notes of citrus rind, Meyer lemon, Yellow apple, and honeysuckle, layered with honeycomb on the nose. The flavors are marzipan, White nectarine, youthful apple, and lime curd, laced with bright acidity, and a long, mouth-watering finish. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — T.P.

$33 Cedarville Vineyard

Pisces (February 19 – March 20): Chardonnay

Themes: “Pisces is the most intuitive, sensitive, and empathetic sign of the entire zodiac and they will go to great lengths to ensure the happiness of those around them,” says Pitts.

Why: “Chardonnay is a versatile and crowd-pleasing wine, much like the fish. Chardonnay can adapt to different environments, in different regions around the globe. Chardonnay grown in Mendocino Ridge must adapt to the long cold breezes from the nearby ocean, while its counterpart in Livermore Valley gets to bask in the sunshine and enjoy a warm growing season. These regions create completely unique styles of Chardonnay, yet it can please a wide audience, embodying Pisces’s empathetic and caring nature.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

William Fèvre 2023 Vaillons Premier Cru Chardonnay (Chablis)

Crushed stone and green apple mingle on the nose that rests against a wall of baby’s breath and muddled white blossom. The steely palate accentuates purity of fruit while elevating freshness on the finish that is lifted by a nervy layer of acidity. 94 Points — A.C.C.

$93 Wine.com

Presqu’ile Winery 2023 Chardonnay (Santa Maria Valley)

Honeysuckle, lemon-glazed apple and gardenia aromas are very comforting and inviting on the nose of this bottling. There’s a tense landing to the palate, where lemon, lime zest and green apple flavors make for an electric, acid-powered sip. 93 Points — M.K.

$51 Presqu’ile Winery

title: The 8 Most Iconic Cheese Shops in America
summary:
Curious how to tell the difference between a good and great cheese shop? Consider this guide to retailers from New York to Washington State.

The post The 8 Most Iconic Cheese Shops in America appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
There are several ways to determine what makes a cheese shop worth a visit. And as with many things in food and wine, there aren’t simple answers. But, some guidelines can help you find the best cheese shop for your needs.

Cheese educator David Asher believes how a shop engages with its community is paramount. “A great cheese shop makes connections between the cheese producers and consumers and tries to form a relationship between them,” he says.

This connection is part of a larger cultural shift to understand where and how our foods are made. “Cheese stores can act as a liaison between good farmers producing good cheese and their consumers,” he adds.

Additionally, cheese scholar Carlos Yescas says the difference between a good and a great cheese shop often comes down to what’s for sale and how it’s being sold. A retailer worth its salt will seek out products from cheesemakers that share its values. This could mean supporting independent local producers, sourcing rare international labels, and hiring and training staff to become cheese experts. In doing so, these shops become community hubs of cheese exploration.

You’ll know a good cheesemonger when you meet them because they’ll be excited to talk to you about their products and to cut samples for you to taste, says Christine Clark, a writer and cheese educator.

Willingness to give samples is key, she adds. One person’s cheese preference may be different than another’s. Plus, cheese is a living product and can taste different each time you try it. “Whereas wine has vintages by year, in cheese, each day can be like a new vintage,” Clark says.

If you’re ready to explore the evolving world of artisanal cheese, consider visiting one of these eight iconic cheese shops. While they’re certainly not the only destinations for quality cheese in the United States, this list is a great place to start.

Antonelli’s

Austin, Texas

Opened by husband-wife duo John and Kendall Antonelli in 2010, Antonelli’s has grown into a Hyde Park institution with dozens of cheeses cut to order. Plus, you can find charcuterie, pickles, breads, and other sundries. The brightly lit cafe offers custom boards and gift baskets, and its educational program includes everything from Cheese 101 classes to guided tastings featuring pairings such as charcuterie or halloween candy.

Yescas notes that many Austin chefs source ingredients from Antonelli’s and credits the shop with bringing artisanal cheese culture to a new corner of the country. “They’re a catalyst in their state for better cheese,” he says.

Artisan Cheese Company

Sarasota, Florida

One of Clark’s favorite shops, Artisan Cheese Company, opened a small storefront in 2012 and relocated to its current 2,000-square-foot space in Sarasota’s Rosemary District in 2018. Its expansive selection includes such all-American standard-bearers as Jasper Hill and Point Reyes, as well as hard-to-source European producers like Switzerland’s Gourmino and England’s Neal’s Yard. The airy, industrial digs also feature beer, natural wine, salumi, and more, and the café serves grilled cheese, crostini, and other small plates.

Beecher’s Handmade Cheese

Seattle, Washington

While the Pike’s Place location of this Seattle landmark is admittedly thronged with tourists, Beecher’s earns its spot for longevity and influence. The original glass-walled shop opened in 2003 with a then-uncommon commitment to sourcing milk from local cows not fed recombinant bovine growth hormones and hand-making cheese onsite. Today, the original location has since spawned four cafés throughout Washington and several airport outposts worth a visit.

Fairfield Cheese Company

Fairfield, Connecticut

One of Yescas’ top shops is this storefront with “amazing service” and an extensive selection of small-production U.S. and international cheeses. Fairfield stocks cheeses like Jasper Hill Farms’ ultra-seasonal, spruce-wrapped Winnimere cheese, Amsterdammer Betty Koster’s Brabander Reserve, and more.

“The owners are committed to diversity and inclusion in their mongering, and they’re also doing the hard work of connecting cheese enthusiasts to cheese with their tours,” says Yescas. Fairfield Cheese Company offers classes devoted to U.S., French, and other regional cheeses, and hosts trips to explore far-flung cheese cultures, like sojourns to the United Kingdom, called A British Cheese Odyssey.

Formaggio Kitchen

Cambridge, Massachusetts

“People don’t think Boston is a cheese town, but Boston is one of the original cheese towns. Vermont is our local farm,” says Yescas. He hails Formaggio Kitchen as a standard-bearer in the U.S. artisanal cheese movement, noting how the 1978 Cambridge shop not only served as its own importer of then-hard-to-find European cheeses, but also spawned two other Formaggios in the Boston area and one in New York City. In nearly 50 years of operation, Formaggio has introduced generations of northeasterners to specialty cheeses like Valençay frais (the Loire’s ash-coated goat cheese) and Vermont’s esteemed Jasper Hills.

Fromagination

Madison, Wisconsin

Nearly 50% of U.S. specialty cheeses are made in Wisconsin, and dairy is a point of pride for many in the state. Fromagination on Madison’s Capitol Hill celebrates the local bounty with an extensive collection of Wisconsin labels including Uplands Cheese and Bleu Mont Dairy, plus national and international selections like Norwegian Gjetost and Germany’s crowd-pleasing blue cheese, Cambozola.

Milkfarm

Los Angeles, California

Natural wine and high-end pantry items, like Jacobsen sea salt, line the walls of this well-stocked shop in Los Angeles’ Eagle Rock neighborhood. One of Asher’s favorites, Milkfarm specializes in cheeses from small and independent producers primarily in the L.A. area. It also offers made-to-order sandwiches—including a cult grilled cheese—plus baked goods and cheese boards to enjoy at the counter or sunny sidewalk seating.

Saxelby Cheesemongers

New York, New York

When legendary cheesemaker, educator, and author Anne Saxelby opened Saxelby Cheesemongers in Manhattan’s Chelsea Market in 2006, it was hailed as New York City’s first store dedicated to American-made farmstead and artisanal cheese. Asher and Clark are among the many cheese pros who still sing its praises, citing its friendly atmosphere and knowledgeable cheesemongers who happily cut samples and talk through options with curious customers.

Honorable Mentions

As valuable as cheese shops can be, they aren’t the only places to find great cheese.

“Consider shopping for cheese at a local farmers market, where some of the best small cheese producers sell their stuff,” says Asher. “Some makers, for example, my favorite natural cheesemaker in America, Bobolink Dairy, sell exclusively at NYC-area farmers’ markets.”

Additionally, specialty grocers like Rainbow Grocery in San Francisco and Philadelphia’s Di Bruno Bros. have destination-worthy cheese selections among other gourmet goods.

title: Wine Enthusiast’s 27th Annual Wine Star Award Nominees
summary:
The Wine Star Awards honor individuals and companies making outstanding contributions to the wine and spirits industry.

The post Wine Enthusiast’s 27th Annual Wine Star Award Nominees appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
This year marks the 27th annual Wine Star Awards, honoring the individuals and companies that make outstanding contributions to the wine and beverage industry. Here are the nominees across 11 of the 17 categories for the 2026 Awards.

The winners of these categories will be featured in the magazine’s Best of Year issue and celebrated at our annual black-tie gala in January 2027. The winners for the additional categories—Person of the Year, Wine & Culture Award, American Wine Legend, Lifetime Achievement Award, American Wine Region of the Year, and International (Non-U.S.) Wine Region of the Year—will be named and also honored at the gala. We salute all of the dedicated beverage professionals who have flourished this year.

The Process

All full-time and contributing divisions of the Wine Enthusiast media team, including sales, events, marketing, and editorial, were invited to submit nominees for the 2026 Wine Star Awards categories. Nominations were submitted with explanations of what made the submission appropriate for consideration. The list of potential nominees was then sent to the group for anonymous voting to cull the list down. Finalists were chosen from the culled-down list by the executive media team with selections based on many factors, including impact on consumers and trade in the wine and spirits space; commercial successes; company/brand vision; and trendsetting.

The Wine Enthusiast Wine Star Awards are an overall beverage industry awards program. While the editors are invited to participate, this is a collaborative program incorporating the input of all divisions of our company and is not solely an editorial franchise.

American Winery of the Year

Pine Ridge Vineyards

Napa, CA

While many Napa winemakers rely on Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay, Pine Ridge Vineyards (and its winemaker Joshua Mendoza-Widaman) would rather praise the valley’s Chenin Blanc and Viognier. Those plots were planted 30 years ago as an homage to the past—Chenin was widely planted in the ‘60s and ‘70s. Today, Pine Ridge’s Chenin Blanc and Viognier blend is tapped into what today’s drinkers want: lower-calorie, lower-alcohol, low-sugar, and vegan wines served in lightweight, carbon footprint-friendly bottles. Next up: going net-zero by 2050.

Chalk Hill Estate Vineyards

Sonoma County, CA

In 1972, a San Francisco attorney took a bet on a natural amphitheater, carved into the chalky white hills in Eastern Sonoma. Fifty years later and his wager has paid off in spades. The wild, 1,300-acre Chalk Hill property—and its self-named AVA—helped set the standard for Sonoma Chardonnay in the ‘80s. So much so that clonal studies from UC Davis identified a rare proprietary Chardonnay clone, Chalk Hill Clone 97. Chalk Hill also partners with the Court of Master Sommeliers to fund a scholarship for women looking to further their careers in wine.

Lytle-Barnett

Eola-Amity Hills, OR

In the Willamette Valley, the land of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Lytle-Barnett commits to bubbles. Brand founder Andy Lytle staunchly believed that the volcanic and sedimentary soils of his stretch of Eola-Amity Hills could produce Champagne-quality sparkling wine. And he was correct. Lytle Barnett’s exacting sparklers are all estate-grown, produced in the Champagne method, riddled and disgorged on site and aged on the lees until the wine is ready to be released. Lytle is also a co-founder of Method Oregon, a group that sets strict quality guardrails on all Oregon sparkling production.

Grgich Hills Estate

Napa, CA

During the Judgement of Paris, the 1973 Chardonnay made by Milijenko “Mike” Grgich (then winemaker at Chateau Montelena) helped solidify Napa’s place on the world stage. His own brand, Grgich Hills Estate (celebrating 50 years in 2027), continues to carry forward that legacy. A staunch dedication to single-vineyard, often old vine or vines cultivated on original rootstock, flexes a dedication to Napa history. A 10-toes-down approach to organic and regenerative agriculture shows a commitment to Napa’s future. Grgich is still entirely family-owned and -operated, and its Chardonnay remains quintessential.

Penns Woods Winery

Brandywine Valley, PA

Proving that excellence can exist from coast to coast, Penns Woods produces terroir-driven wines rooted in more than four decades of viticulture. Italian-born founder Gino Razzi made wine in Abruzzo before setting his sights on his adopted home of Pennsylvania, where he found an abandoned vineyard first planted in the late 1970s. Today, old-vine plantings remain at the Chadds Ford Estate Vineyard, anchoring an estate program devoted to expressing the character of Pennsylvania-grown wine. As Penns Woods celebrates its 25th anniversary, winemaker Davide Creato crafts small-lot wines including Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, and Viognier, while next-gen family member Carley Razzi leads the winery into its next chapter.

Environmental Advocate of the Year

Louisa Rose

Head of Sustainability, Hill-Smith Family Estates | Australia

Long before Al Gore uttered the words “global warming,” Louisa Rose was pushing through aggressive, ambitious environmental initiatives. For every planted acre, Hill-Smith Family Estates (which includes Yalumba, Pewsey Vale, Jansz, and Smith & Hooper wineries) has 1.2 acres of native vegetation. Over the last 15 years, the company has reduced greenhouse gas emissions by 41%.

Rose and the Yalumba team oversee one of Australia’s most vital nurseries and are the custodians of some of the country’s oldest vines, protected under the world’s first Old Vine Charter (which, Yalumba put into motion). All these efforts show that sustainability can be achieved on a large scale.

WineStone Group

Portugal

While WineStone Group has expanded rapidly over the last few years, picking up brands and properties across Portugal to reach production levels of 12 million bottles a year, it never abandoned its sustainability goals. Water is a big focus—WineStone participates in water-reuse research and extensive water stewardship initiatives. Vineyards are largely organic, or have achieved integrated vineyard certification. WineStone’s long-term sustainability roadmap, which includes air-tight ESG supplier auditing, will guide efforts as the group continues to future-proof.

Varvaglione 1921

Puglia, Italy

When one thinks of Italian grapes, Susumaniello and Negroamaro are likely not the first that come to mind. But for the Varvaglione family, the indigenous Puglian varieties represent their heritage. The fourth-generation winery is dedicated to preserving and promoting their home-team grapes. In an effort to preserve history and explore climate resiliency, the Puglian winery opened its biodiversity vineyard: an experimental field that hosts over 500 Mediterranean and Balkan grape varieties. Also on the docket: intense renewable energy investments and publishing their sustainability research.

Domaine Carneros

Napa Valley, California

Domaine Carneros is an American outpost of the Taittinger family’s sparkling wine holdings with a strong commitment to sustainability. Solar panels were put in two decades ago—long before it was a norm. Domaine Carneros was an early subscriber to Napa Green, the California Sustainable Winegrowing Alliance, and Fish Friendly Farming. Solar efforts have expanded to include a solar microgrid that generates up to 80% of the winery’s electricity needs. Wastewater from production is recycled to irrigate vineyards, which are abundant and diverse thanks to cover crops, native plants, and owl boxes. All these initiatives are an effort to further the legacy of the sparkling wine legend Eileen Crane, who passed away earlier this year.

Benziger Winery

Sonoma Valley, California

In the year 2000, Benziger became the very first winery in either Sonoma or Napa to receive its biodynamic certification. Now, every vineyard they source from is certified sustainable, organic, or biodynamic. They view the estate as an ecosystem—not only the vines must thrive but the soil, the sheep, highland cattle, owls, bluebirds, insects, and plants that live in and line the vines. Efforts like tram tours to see their vineyards, insectary, and olive grove help teach guests what sustainability looks like in practice.

European Winery of the Year

Champagne Laurent-Perrier

Marne, France

Champagne Laurent-Perrier is persistently one of the best-selling wine brands in the United States and a darling of somms everywhere. Primarily, it’s because the maison remains ahead of trends. In 1889, Laurent-Perrier launched the first commercially successful Grand Vin Sans Sucre—a century and a half before low-dosage came into style. They’ve bet big on rosé aged for years on lees, and multi-vintage wines like Grand Siècle, their top cuvée. It’s born from blending single cru, single-grape wines from three different vintages, which is an exercise in precision, but also a way to create the perfect cuvée in an ever-changing climate. Innovations continue—the maison has invested heavily in VitiBot, a line of autonomous vineyard robots.

Ravasqueira

Alentejo, Portugal

Ravasqueira’s Alentejo estate perfectly balances Portuguese history with its future—moving forward while maintaining an irreverence for the past. They work with iconic Alentejo grapes: Touriga Nacional, Alicante Bouschet, Arinto. At their 7,000-acre estate (owned by the José de Mello family legacy) they welcome guests with a warm sense of hospitality and send them home as ambassadors of Alentejo wine. Forward-thinking vineyard practices, including the use of drones in the vineyard, have an eye on the future.

Domaine Lafage

Roussillon, France

Seven generations in, Domaine Lafage has found that it’s rather easy being green. The Roussillon estate was one of the first in the world to achieve a Regenerative Viticulture Association certification. They will list off buzzwords like soil revitalization, biodiverse ecosystems, carbon sequestration, indigenous variety introduction, and anti-industrial agriculture, but their acolytes are drawn to their wines for the site-specific winemaking, freshness, and shining minerality—which is rare, in the hot, dry Mediterranean pocket. In a region known for fortified wines, Domaine Lafage makes expressive, balanced wines of extreme value.

Quinta do Paral

Alentejo, Portugal

Over the last year, Quinta do Paral has infiltrated a handful of new international markets. Its success strategy? Break down Portugal’s American reputation as a value-centric region and show off the luxury side of Alentejo. Paral recently opened a high-end hotel on the property, complete with fine dining and a flush hospitality experience. Splashiness aside, the winery has a reverence for the old: the Morszeck family recently acquired the oldest vineyard in DO Vidigueira, planted in 1918, and plans to carry it forward. Many other Alentejo traditions remain, including using indigenous varieties and aging in talhas de barro clay pots.

Avignonesi

Tuscany, Italy

What was Virginie Saverys’ mission when she acquired this historic Vino Nobile di Montepulciano producer in 2009? Lean even further into the Tuscan terroir. Avignonesi is now the largest biodynamic estate in all of Italy, and landed its B Corp Certification in 2022. Sangiovese is still a focus—this is Montepulciano—but Avignonesi has welcomed in Cannaiolo, Colorino, Ciliegiolo, and Mamolo to build out its native varieties. All efforts go forward with a focus on ethical agriculture, cultural responsibility, and a caretaker mentality—fitting, as their property has a 500-year-history of grape growing.

Importer of the Year

T. Edward Wines & Spirits

New York

Their wine book reads like a checklist of cool-kid producers and revered modernists: Mallorca’s 4 Kilos, Burgundy’s Armand Heitz, Champagne Billecart-Salmon, Spain’s Gulp Hablo, and Napa’s Scarecrow. The spirits side is equally padded (Empirical, Faccia Brutto, Yola Mezcal). This in-touch and passionate portfolio, supported by a savvy team of sales folks and marketing pros, helped T. Edward see explosive sales in the midst of an industry-wide slump. Proof: Despite the challenges the overall industry faced, 2025 marked a year of record-breaking revenue (38% year-over-year) and growth for the team.

Bertrand’s Wines

New York

Why be a Jack of all trades when you can be a master of one? For Bertrand Leulliette of Bertrand’s Wines, that’s Burgundy. The team spends three months a year tasting, meeting vignerons, exploring the region, drinking through restaurant menus, and unearthing new gems in under-represented appellations to bring Burgundy’s next big star to American soil. Despite the sky-high prices Burgundy is now associated with, the book is full of deep-cuts and hidden gems, all priced approachably. Half the portfolio highlights female-owned wineries or female vignerons.

Polaner Selections

New York

Doug Polaner is the man behind the New York City wine menu. Over the last 25 years, Polaner Selections has curated a list of influential, sought-after winemakers which, in turn, has diversified and enriched the New York market—names like Selosse, Dagueneau, Emidio Pepe, and Roagna. The portfolio knows no geographic boundaries or price thresholds—they merely seek to excite and intrigue wine drinkers with quality producers making quality wines. That said, an overarching thread between all producers is a commitment to bettering the earth.

Ethica Wines

Miami

A global importing powerhouse with a staunch focus on premium Italian wines. A 70-person sales force across the country (and the continent, and in Asia) has been preaching the gospel of Italian wine for a decade to consumers, media, and trade. The latter arm runs more than 500 industry events a year.

This year marked Ethica’s 10th anniversary, and it’s already a banner one: 2025 pulled in $140 million in revenue, a 20% increase compared to 2024. The company expects to reach $165 million in revenue in 2026—a true feat in the midst of inflation and tariffs.

Mary Taylor Wines

Connecticut

At a glance, Mary Taylor’s portfolio looks homogenous: all bottles have the same, simple white label bearing the appellation and her name. There’s a reason for such monotony—Taylor’s goal is to make the rich, but complex, tapestry of European wines more approachable to the everyday drinker. She prioritizes independent producers playing with lesser-known grapes in non-banner regions, AOCs, DOCS, or DOs. Wines are largely priced under $20 a bottle. Nine years in, people trust her name—Mary Taylor Wines is now a multi-million dollar brand.

Innovator of the Year

Gallo, Single Serve 200 mL Tetra Packs

California, United States

In a time when wine has more competition than ever, Gallo doubled down on a smart strategy: put their wine in single-serve, resealable, sustainable, $2 TetraPacks. To stick the landing, the wine giant invested significant time and money into making the packaging and technology. Gallo’s tried, tested, and now-perfected TetraPacks house wines from Barefoot, Mark West, and Clos du Bois allow the brands to show up at festivals, events, and convenience stores. Their plan is working: In-house research shows the majority of TetraPack buyers had not consumed wine in over a year.

Chase Renton

Winemaker-founder, Resilience Wine & L’Angolo Estate | Willamette Valley, Oregon

In 2017, Oregon winemaker Chase Renton underwent a gauntlet of challenges. First, a cancer diagnosis and chemotherapy. Then came burnout, anxiety, and depression. As he pulled through, he reached back to help others. All of the proceeds from his wine, Resilience, a Dundee Hills Pinot Noir, go towards Kevin Love Fund, the NBA star’s organization that supports mental health awareness, research, and education. To Renton, Resilience is a reminder that wine brings people together.

Dr. Laura Catena

Vintner, Bodega Catena Zapata | Mendoza, Argentina

Many people are introduced to Laura Catena through her wines: smart reds and whites that reflect the terroir at Argentina’s high-altitude vineyards. Many more people know her through her advocacy and leadership. She’s put money and time into Argentina’s viticulture research, preservation of the country’s old vines, and mentoring the country’s next-generation. With her background in medicine, Catena has spoken openly about the true relationship between health and wine consumption at a time when the neo-prohibitionist movement is louder than ever.

Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger

Founder, French Bloom | Limoux, France

When Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger, former director of the Michelin Guide, married a winemaker, one would expect her to produce, well, a wine. She’s done that, but not by conventional standards: French Bloom is a terroir-driven, Limoux-made sparkling wine without a drop of alcohol. Everyone from models to Michelin-starred chefs have embraced the wines, which include a sparkling white, a rosé, a zero-dosage, and a Vintage-style sparkler. This fall, French Bloom will open an estate in Limoux—the first non-alcoholic wine brand in the world to have its own maison.

Elizabeth Higley

Head Winemaker, Windsor Run Cellars | North Carolina, USA

Ask a North Carolina winemaker who is the backbone of the state’s budding industry, and they’ll point to Elizabeth Higley. As Head Winemaker at Windsor Run Cellars, she lends her knowledge to small and emerging wineries who use her custom crush and production services. At her own label, Demarcation Wine Co., she directs all proceeds to a Women in Wine Education Scholarship at a local community college viticulture program. Higley also helped establish the North Carolina Winegrowers Collective—an initiative tackling the viticultural challenges of the American Southeast.

New World Winery of the Year

Te Mata

Hawke’s Bay, New Zealand

Founded in 1892 by English immigrants, Te Mata Estate has become the north star for New Zealand winemaking. Coleraine, an age-worthy, Bordeaux-style blend born from an assemblage of plots, with the oldest planted in 1892, would surely rank as a “Grand Cru,” should that system exist in New Zealand. Their secret? Listening to the land. Their historic vineyards, perched in rocky outcrops on the slopes of Te Mata Peak, are lovingly maintained.

Leeuwin Estate

Margaret River, Australia

Leeuwin Estate, one of Margaret River’s founding wineries, is a beacon for Aussie Chardonnay, Cabernet, and Riesling. The estate’s mission has always been ambitious: to make wines that could rank among the best in the world, while expressing the character of Margaret River. Leeuwin is now known for precise, age-worthy wines and the oldest Chardonnay vines in the region. Their Art Series remains one of Australia’s most collectible wines.

Bodegas Salentein

Uco Valley, Argentina

While big names now congregate in Argentina’s Uco Valley, the region was once barren. Mijndert Pon was always a believer. He planted vines 1,700 meters up the valley’s slopes, when the region was still a gamble, and made cool-climate, high-altitude Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Chardonnay. Now, San Pablo is one of the country’s most coveted vine growing regions. In 2019, San Pablo received its official Geographic Indication status, largely thanks to efforts from José Galante, Bodegas Salentein’s chief winemaker and the Father of Argentine Malbec.

Viña Don Melchor

Alto Maipo, Chile

This vanguard Chilean winery possesses an unwavering dedication to excellence. The scores are consistently high (this year, Don Melchor produced the highest-scoring Chilean wine in Wine Enthusiast history), and the estate’s followers have long been enamored by its vision. In 1883, Don Melchor saw the viticultural potential of the Maipo Valley, and imagined high-quality European vineyards in its foothills. He imported vines from France, planted them, watched over them, and 150 years later, these vines produce stellar wines that have set the standard for Chilean Cabernet.

Karas Wines

Ararat Valley, Armenia

While Armenia is the origin of the oldest-known grape specimens in the world, the region doesn’t always get its due respect. Karas, Armenia’s largest commercial winery, is shifting that perspective. Over the last 22 years, their love for Armenia’s wine scene has brought the category from niche curiosity to mass-market distribution. They did so by bringing in Michel Rolland to raise the region’s quality standards and by pounding the pavement, heading to Wine Paris (the country’s first appearance) and around the U.S. to sell the story of Armenian landscapes and viticultural history. Now, Armenia is one of the top 25 wine importing countries to the United States.

Sommelier/Beverage Director of the Year

Jorge Riera

Wine Director | Frenchette Group | New York, NY

Wine lovers in New York may recognize some of Jorge Riera’s resume highlights. He led the all-French list at Balthazar and Ten Bells’ new-wave natural selection, alongside benchmark programs at Wildair and Contra. Today, he’s handling the wine program at the Frenchette Group, which started as a bistro in Tribeca and has since swollen to include Le Rock, Le Veau d’Or, and Wild Cherry. His disciples follow him for his explorative and globe-trotting but exacting approach to natural wine. As Frenchette Group’s venues continue to collect recognition from James Beard and 50 Best, it’s clear Riera’s role is a partial driving force.

Laura Santander

Sommelier, Co-Owner | Hermitage | Mexico City, MX

Mexico City’s Laura Santander knows that a sommelier’s role isn’t just on the floor. It’s out in the market and, crucially, online. Via Instagram, she shares her day-to-day as a somm-slash-educator with over 80,000 followers. At resorts and hotels around Mexico, she runs bilingual educational events to spread the gospel of Mexican wine, allowing tourists to expand their drink knowledge beyond margaritas. In what little spare time she has, she judges international wine competitions and is a partner in Hermitage, an education-center-slash-event venue in Mexico City.

Alex Cuper

Wine Director | El Che and Brasero | Chicago, IL

At El Che, a Chicago bastion of beef, Alex Cuper curates an extensive list of entirely South American wines: a passionate assortment of sparkling, white, red wines, and magnums from Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, and Brazil. Over at Brasero, he flips the script and stocks exclusively 100 wines under $100. The latter acts as an approachable on-ramp to the world of South American wine—skin-contact wines from Uruguay, chilled reds from Argentina. The former proves that South American wines are woefully underrated in the American market.

Nikita Malhotra

Partner-Beverage Director | Smithereens | New York, NY

Nikita Malhotra’s rotating list isn’t diverse, nor is there breadth. There are no Napa Cabs next to Spanish reds. Instead, every menu focuses on one specific region or variety. Smithereens opened with a forensic deep dive into Riesling. Then came the all-Grenache menu, followed by sake, Chenin, and Champagne themes. The approach reflects her deep desire to explore, share, learn, and grow, for both her and everyone who walks through the door. (Notably, her parents owned an Upper East Side bottle shop.) Staff picks are scrawled in pen; the glass pours are generous. One rule is that Riesling is always available.

William Simons

Director of Operations, Wine Director | Albi | Washington, DC

Napa and Burgundy be damned. At Albi, Williams Simons commits fully to the Levantine wines (and, more broadly, those from Armenia and Georgia). Which isn’t an easy feat—it often involves DM-ing producers to arrange samples and moving wines from Palestine across the Israeli border. Worth it, to him, to prove there’s room for Middle Eastern wines in the world of American fine dining. Impassioned and serious as the menu seems, it’s balanced out by quirky, passionate essays and fun facts.

Spirit Brand of the Year

Cazcanes Tequila

Tequila, Mexico

It takes a lot of chutzpah to start a tequila brand in 2026—the category is crowded with celebrity-backed bottles. Luckily, Cazcanes has what it takes to break through the noise. This year, their Nuestras Raíces agave distillate was the first spirit in history to receive a perfect 100-point score for Wine Enthusiast—a landmark not only for the category, but for the spirits industry as a whole, considering that the publication evaluates over 25,000 products annually. The secret sauce? An unrelenting dedication to tradition and an uncompromising stance on additive-free tequila.

Manojo Mezcal

Oaxaca, Mexico

If you’re looking to make a great-tasting spirit, why not call up one of the world’s leading experts on flavor? In 2024, chef Enrique Olvera was brought on board to launch a mezcal brand with fifth-generation mezcaleros Joel Velasco and Felicitas Hernández. The new brand’s strategy is to move slowly: wait until all agave is aged just right and crushed with horse-drawn tahonas instead of machinery. The first release received a glowing 95 from Wine Enthusiast for its notes of lightly sweet lychee, lime peel, pink peppercorn, and a smoky exhale.

Lucas Bols

Amsterdam, Netherlands

There are historic spirits brands and then there’s Amsterdam-based Lucas Bols, who in 2025 celebrated their 450-year anniversary. A lot has changed in the last four centuries: the Dutch distiller’s portfolio includes 20-plus brands, from non-alcoholic trailblazer Fleure to Tequila Partida. As they acquire and expand, their mantra maintains that they meet drinkers where they are, evident in programming like the Lucas Bols Cocktail Academy—an effort to educate, interact with, and onboard more consumers.

Middle West Spirits

Columbus, Ohio

Columbus is slowly becoming a major player in the whiskey world thanks to Middle West Spirits, who oversees almost two dozen brands. 2024 marked the opening of a 75,000-square-foot distillery, which ramped up production and ultimately allowed them to snap up Old Elk in 2025. Outside of Old Elk, Middle West has partnerships with over 20 brands, making it a rival of some of the biggest spirits production houses in the country, and one of the most important grain-to-glass producers in the nation. Their home products are the heart of production—things like Pumpernickel rye whiskey and single-grain, ultra-aged expressions.

Teremana Tequila

Jalisco, Mexico

Regardless of whether or not you consider Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson a true spirits icon, the brand is crushing: a second distillery is opening soon to meet Teremana‘s booming demand. The success is partly brokered by Johnson’s celebrity status, but equally supported by the success of the stratospheric tequila category (and, the support of owner-distritributor Mast-Jägermeister). The tequila is always solid—it’s made with the Lopez family, tequila region icons, in the highest heights of the Jalisco highlands.

Wine Executive of the Year

Shilah Salmon

SVP of Marketing | The Duckhorn Portfolio | Napa, CA

Shilah Salmon knows that big-spending wine buyers aren’t just sitting in wine bars. As the SVP of Marketing at Jackson Family Wines, she led the marketing execution of the La Crema partnership with the WNBA and partnered with numerous Pride events around the U.S., bringing in new drinkers, sparking new wine occasions, and driving growth. In her current role as SVP of Marketing at The Duckhorn Portfolio (Duckhorn Vineyards, Kosta Browne, Calera, Goldeneye), she turns lifestyle-luxury brands into sought-after names. Beyond her 9-to-5, Salmon co-founded “Beyond the Headlines,” an industry-wide initiative that helps reframe and contextualize the industry’s challenges.

Karissa Kruse

CEO | Sonoma County Winegrowers | Sonoma County, CA

Karissa Kruse plays a vital role in Sonoma. As the CEO of Sonoma County Winegrowers, Kruse has helped the region earn the title of one of the most sustainable in the world and has spoken at conferences around the globe on the topic. She’s drawn in new drinkers by leading Sonoma County to partner with the San Francisco Giants in a first-of-its-kind partnership. For her next act, Kruse is the new co-owner of Dutton-Goldfield Winery in the Russian River Valley with her husband, Steve Dutton.

José Alberto Zuccardi

Director | Familia Zuccardi | Argentina

When José Alberto Zuccardi joined his family business in 1985, Argentina didn’t really exist on the global wine stage. That didn’t matter—he travelled the world, selling the story and quality of Argentinian Malbec. At the same time, he built infrastructure to keep Argentina’s industry moving forward, investing in education programs for workers and their families, zeroing in on the best terroir possible, and raising the bar for quality. He looked to what was working in California and Europe, setting up irrigation, ramping up exports, and moving away from big bulk wine. Argentina is all the better for it.

Rick Bonitati

President, CEO | Kopf Family Estates | Napa, CA

Sequoia Grove is a historic Rutherford AVA estate and a pioneer in the Napa Valley, and it’s undergone a remarkable transformation under Rick Bonitati’s leadership. When Bonitati joined Kopf Family (Sequoia Grove, St. Francis Winery & Vineyards, Résonance) in 2018, fresh from senior roles at Paul Hobbs Wine and Jackson Family, he launched vineyard development projects, acquisitions, and sustainability efforts like 100% renewable energy adoption, achieving Napa Green certification. He’s put his energy into wildfire relief, land conservation, and even service dog programming. Under his guidance, the Sequoia Grove legacy is stronger than ever.

David Skurnik and Oren Simon

President and CEO | Skurnik Wine & Spirits | New York, NY

In the midst of industry-wide downturns and consolidation, David Skurnik and Oren Simon are doubling down and riding the inflection point. The second-gen leadership took over as President and CEO of the importer-distributor in 2025 after over a decade, rising from customer service and controller roles. Now, they’re carrying forward their luxury portfolio and padding out their ranks with a dedicated team, and taking bets on forward-thinking producers and alternative vessels (like wine in kegs).

Winemaker of the Year

Jeffrey Grosset

Clare Valley, Australia

Jeffrey Grosset loves an underdog. He is Australia’s unofficial King of Riesling—an outlier in a country known more for red wines—and advocated for screw caps long before they became commonplace. Grosset is beloved for his single-vineyard bottlings, with Polish Hill and Springvale among his most iconic wines. A leader in organic and biodynamic farming, Grosset remains one of the only producers in Clare Valley to hold both certifications.

Matheson Worrell and Katy Kidd

Jonesville, NC

Born-and-bread North Carolinians Katy Kidd and Matheson Worrel are evangelists for the wines of the American South. The Blue Ridge Mountains are primed for wine, they promise, and they’re doing an excellent job telling that story at Dynamis. They’ve established regional standards, built out a portfolio of luxury wines, and raked in high scores for their Bordeaux-style blends born from vineyards 1,640 feet above sea level in the Swan Creek AVA.

Paolo Saracco

Piedmont, Italy

Welcome to Moscato’s artisan era. Paolo Saracco, the “Maestro del Moscato,” takes the traditional category and manipulates it into an ultra-craft, highly nerdy process. The gist of his process: 15 districts are treated like crus, vinified separately to best express terroir. Everything is fermented in small batches to maintain freshness and consistency. Geek-tendencies aside, the wines are built for mass pleasure—low-alcohol, food-friendly, crowd-pleasing blends that inspire a new generation of drinkers to pop a cork.

Hans Nittnaus

Burgenland, Austria

After 50 vintages, Hans Nittnaus of the winery Anita & Hans Nittnaus has solidified his role as one of Austria’s leading veteran winemakers. Neusiedlersee locals will confirm that he’s one of the most experienced active winemakers in Austria (and, arguably, the world), but his efforts don’t stop in his vineyard. Nittnaus founded the biodynamic group Pannobile 30 years ago in an effort to fuel debate, experimentation, and community among like-minded growers.

Andrea Ferreyra

Uco Valley, Argentina

Andrea Ferreyra oversees the Uco Valley’s very first winery, Finca La Celia, which was planted in 1890. With over two decades of experience at Argentina’s top wineries, she leads with finesse and a focus on Argentina’s climate and soil, which she translates into wines of exceptional purity. Elegance, precision, and a commitment to place are Ferreyra’s calling cards—her wines consistently bring in acclaim and high scores, proving that the Andes can turn out premium Malbec and Cabernet Franc.

RTD of the Year

Phony Negroni

Brooklyn, NY

Even after all the recent innovation in the non-alcoholic space, some zero-proof drinks can be lackluster. Not the Phony Negroni. Brooklyn distillery St. Agrestis applied its amaro expertise to the N/A category, making a single-serve, bottled negroni packed with juniper, citrus, and a Negroni’s signature bittersweet kick, sans the alcohol. It was such a hit that St. Agrestis has expanded its range to include zero-proof espresso negronis, mezcal negronis, white negronis, and limone negronis. All this proves that aperitivo hour is for everyone.

Tip Top Proper Cocktails

Atlanta, GA

With no bar experience under their belts, music industry vets Yoni Reisman and Neal Cohen saw an opening: A big demand for ready-to-drink real cocktails, but no brands answering the call. So they tapped a James Beard-nominated bartender and launched Tip Top, a range of spirit-forward, 3.4-ounce, well mixed cocktails. Their gamble paid off, and Tip Top is now sold across the country. Resting on laurels they are not—the brand is bringing in more big-name bartenders to help them make quality cocktails at scale.

Juice Runners by Run The Jewels 

United States

Hip-hop duo Run The Jewels are unlikely front-runners in the race to make RTDs better, but we’re glad they’re here. What began as a passion for collaborating with Black-owned breweries on tour evolved into a desire to build their own beverage company, rooted in partnerships with craft producers. That vision became Juice Runners, launched by Killer Mike and El-P in 2025 with Paloma REMIX, a grapefruit mezcal cocktail. It’s more than a celebrity co-sign: The duo has shown up at Tales of the Cocktail, closed a $2 million seed round, and is expanding with Sea Legs, a rum-based cocktail, plus a collaboration with spirits expert Fred Minnick.

Barker Company

Pennsylvania, USA

Creamy, coffee-spiked espresso martinis now come in cans and bottles. We have fashion photographer Nigel Barker and industry vet Philippe Roederer to thank. In 2024, the duo set out to capture the velvet texture, fluffiness, and spirit of a well-made espresso martini. Barker Company‘s quality is uncompromising: made with 100% organic Colombian coffee, caramelized brown sugar, and six-time-distilled vodka that received a rare 93-point score from our spirits reviewer. Simply pour over ice or shake for a perfect-every-time cocktail.

The Finnish Long Drink

New York, NY

This beloved Scandinavian cocktail traces its origins back to the 1952 Helsinki Winter Olympics. The mix of gin, grapefruit, and soda was later canned by a group of Finns and brought into the mainstream. Easy and breezy, crisp and effervescent, and available in zero-sugar, flavored, and extra-strong versions, the drink attracted celebrities like Miles Teller and Kygo to come aboard as early investors. That backing helped the brand grow at a rapid clip—The Finnish Long Drink has tripled in size since 2022, moving 3.3 million nine-liter cases in 2025. Earlier this year, White Claw owners Mark Anthony Group snapped up the brand.

title: 25 Years After 9/11, the NYC Restaurant That Sat Atop the North Tower Remains an Icon
summary:
A new CNN documentary recounts the rise and fall of the legendary World Trade Center restaurant, Windows on the World.

The post 25 Years After 9/11, the NYC Restaurant That Sat Atop the North Tower Remains an Icon appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
This year marks 25 years since the September 11 attacks and a new CNN documentary recounts the rise and fall of the iconic restaurant in the World Trade Center. Premiering on September 7, Top of the World commemorates Windows on the World, perched on the 106th and 107th floors of the North Tower, and its destruction in 2001. The 40-minute film features firsthand accounts from staff members including day-one wine director Kevin Zraly, hostess Nathalie Tolentino, prep cook Sekou Siby, and fine-dining chef—and native New Yorker—Michael Lomonaco.

Top of the World charts the restaurant’s origins: Windows on the World opened in 1976 and was conceived as a marketing effort, a way to humanize the newly built Twin Towers. The Port Authority, the operators of the Towers, turned to legendary restaurateur Joe Baum of Tavern on the Green in Central Park and The Rainbow Room at Rockefeller Plaza, who was determined to make Windows on the World iconic from opening day. 

And it was.

Originally designed by the architect Warren Platner, it was a symbol of American optimism spread out over two floors and 50,000 square feet. Wherever you sat, you had a view of Manhattan below. Everything and everyone, from the patrons who dined there to the logo illustrated by Milton Glaser, was glamorous and stylish. Dinner was a spectacle and the staff uniforms were costumes for the sky-high stage. James Beard created the food menu, which was accompanied by the biggest wine list New York City had ever seen. New York magazine deemed it “the most spectacular restaurant in the world” and Windows went on to become the highest-grossing restaurant in the country. 

“Baum really was a visionary in so many ways,” Chef Michael Lomonaco tells Wine Enthusiast. “To put a restaurant on top of a building like that was unheard of. There weren’t a lot of buildings that had restaurants on higher floors—anywhere.” 

Lomonaco says what made Windows on the World so distinct was its massive space, the incredible views, and the genuinely warm hospitality offered by a diverse staff. He recalls the restaurant on the 106th floor and the bar on the 107th. The latter went through a few different iterations with names like The Greatest Bar on Earth and Cellar in the Sky. When Lomonaco was hired in the late ’90s, the bar became a wine-focused restaurant called Wild Blue. 

Windows on the World had something for everyone, the chef says: “You had private dining spaces, big rooms, small rooms,” Lomonaco says. “There were weddings and bar mitzvahs and corporate events there. New Year’s Eve celebrations. The bar itself seated 300 people!” 

The restaurant team came from countries all over the globe, including Peru, India, Morocco, and Côte d’Ivoire. As Lomonaco puts it, “It was like the United Nations of the restaurant world.” 

At any given time, Windows had upwards of 500 employees, including cooks, porters, and waitstaff. Because they served breakfast early in the morning and drinks after dinner at night, people worked at Windows around the clock, and there were many roles that helped operations run smoothly. “At our annual holiday party, the people who worked there would bring family members. There would be a thousand people at Windows.” 

Eventually in the 1980s, Baum gave up management of Windows, with various hotel companies co-managing it. Toward the end of that decade, as the documentary chronicles, Windows became a tourist trap. When the World Trade Center bombing happened in 1993, Windows closed for three years to renovate. Baum was asked by the Port Authority to come back for the 1996 reopening and Baum chose Lomonaco, a young star chef who had worked at 21 Club, to revamp the menu and culinary operations, and he joined the Windows staff in 1997. 

At the time of his hire as chef/director, Lomonaco says, the Windows kitchens were in need of reorganization and a new game plan. It paid off: in a New York Times review of Windows, which came out on December 31, 1997, the critic Ruth Reichl awarded the restaurant  two stars and wrote that “Lomonaco’s food at Windows was nearly worthy of the view.” The chef was very appreciative of the recognition, remembering it well nearly 30 years later. 

“We had a great run, from ’97 until the end—the heyday,” Lomonaco says. “A two-star review from the New York Times was excellent! Considering that we served 600 people a night? I was thrilled. Reichl came in during the busiest time—between Thanksgiving and Christmas—to review us. It was a highlight of my career.” 

Then came the morning of September 11: There were 79 employees and 91 guests present at Windows on the World for breakfast service during the terrorist attacks. The team had been preparing for a 25th anniversary party to be thrown in October. The wine director Kevin Zraly had pre-ordered 500 cases of a special-labeled Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label. A few bottles remain today; one is housed at the Smithsonian.

Within a week of September 11, Lomonaco and a cohort of hospitality industry leaders gathered to create Windows of Hope, a charitable organization and relief fund that raised tens of millions of dollars to support the families of Windows staffers who died in the attacks.  

Despite offers to work elsewhere in the country, Lomonaco dug in his heels and stayed in New York. Now  25 years after the attacks and 50 years since Windows opened, Lomonaco is still in New York City, at the helm of Brasserie Cognac Américain, a large splashy restaurant near Bryant Park, and continues to love what he does. Hospitality is his métier, he says, and he’s having fun looking at new projects. 

“I devoted and dedicated my life to the job that I do to honor the memory of those we lost. That’s what the last 25 years has been for me,” Lomonaco says. When he ran Porter House Bar and Grill, a restaurant in Columbus Circle, from 2005 to 2025, he employed former Windows employees. “[Windows] is a constant memory. Through the work I do, I’m able to honor my friends and colleagues.”

title: Franciacorta Is the Sparkling Wine Powerhouse We’ve Been Waiting For
summary:
Writer-at-Large Jeff Porter sits down with Laura Gatti, VP of the Consorzio Franciacorta, to talk tradition, innovation, and bubbles on the WE Podcast.

The post Franciacorta Is the Sparkling Wine Powerhouse We’ve Been Waiting For appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
This episode of the Wine Enthusiast Podcast is brought to you by the Consorzio Franciacorta.

There is a moment in every wine region’s story when reputation catches up to reality. For Franciacorta, that moment arrived, and then kept arriving, year after year. But even with that critical recognition, Franciacorta has remained a wine region that strives to push forward.

Tucked into the hills of Lombardy, south of Lake Iseo, Franciacorta has spent decades doing something quietly radical: building one of Italy’s most serious sparkling wine traditions from the ground up. The region didn’t ride the coattails of a long, storied history—it was awarded DOC status relatively recently, in 1967. Rather, it has earned its place through precision, commitment, and a stubborn belief that this particular stretch of Italian earth had something extraordinary to say.

What sets Franciacorta apart is not just what’s in the glass, but the philosophy behind it. Quality here is not a talking point; it is the organizing principle of the entire denomination. From vineyard management to extended aging requirements, every decision points in the same direction: to the land, its people, and its future. Franciacorta’s forward-thinking winemakers recognize that the wines can only be as good as the soil, vines, and ecosystem that support them, and that future generations deserve to inherit something worth keeping.

In this conversation, Laura Gatti, Vice President of the Consorzio Franciacorta, makes the case for a region that is not standing still. The evolution is deliberate, the ambition is clear, and the wines have never been more compelling.

Franciacorta has always had quality. Now it has the momentum to match.

On Franciacorta’s Unique Geography

Jeff Porter: “So, what’s really interesting about this area is… so you’re kind of in the North-Central part of Italy, and the area was carved out by glaciers moving down the Alps and, you know, big knife cuts of earth and moving down all the way. And it dug out this lake called Lago d’Iseo. The soils are morainic soils. So, think of all the rocks that come from a mountain just being piled up there. And then, there’s this little mountain at the southern edge of the appellation called Monte Orfano, or the ‘Orphan Mountain.’ And basically, think of that as all the dirt that was left after the glacier melted, and it formed its own mountain.

Italy, over time, became part of a sea, and then the sea left, and the sea came back. And so, there’s also some deposits of calcareous, like, fossils and stuff like that. But it’s mainly a morainic soil-based system—really big, like, river stones and stuff like that, good drainage. It’s really kind of a Goldilocks area for making wine.

The other thing that makes it super interesting is that it’s this confluence between the beginning of the foothills of the Alps and a Mediterranean climate, and Lago d’Iseo is kind of the linchpin to all that. You know, it’s a big, deep, deep lake. At some parts of the lake, it’s a thousand feet deep, and so what that allows it to do is be a heat trap. So, the heat goes into the water and doesn’t necessarily stay around the land. It has these really beautiful diurnal shifts, you know, the temperature between day and night. Well, it’ll be warm during the day—it’ll be, like, Mediterranean climate during the day, and then the evening will be cool and alpine, and you get the winds coming down from the mountain. It’s the confluence of the Mediterranean meeting the Alps, which creates a really special place to get ripe grapes, but still maintain that acidity you need for sparkling wine.”

On When and Where to Enjoy Franciacorta

After years of back-and-forth tariff headaches, billions of dollars are back in importer pockets. Are there more worries to come?
